lesson.title: How Far, How Fast: Calculating Propagation Delay
lesson.summary: Propagation delay is the time a signal spends physically traveling across a link, determined purely by the distance it must cover and how fast a signal moves through that particular medium, and it is the single component of latency that no amount of extra bandwidth can ever reduce.
lesson.body:
Latency, as the previous section established, is made up of several distinct delays added together: time spent transmitting a packet onto the link, time spent physically traveling across the medium, time spent waiting in router queues, and time spent being processed at each hop. Propagation delay isolates just the second of these, the pure travel time of a signal moving across a physical medium from one end of a link to the other. It depends on exactly two things: the physical distance the signal must cover, and the speed at which a signal actually propagates through that specific medium, which is always somewhat slower than the speed of light in a vacuum. In fiber optic cable, signals typically travel at roughly two thirds the speed of light in a vacuum, on the order of 2 x 10^8 meters per second, because light moves more slowly through glass than through empty space.

The formula is straightforward: propagation delay equals distance divided by propagation speed. This makes it directly calculable for a real link, which is worth working through once to make the idea concrete. A transatlantic submarine fiber cable connecting New York to London covers a great-circle distance of roughly 5,600 kilometers, or 5,600,000 meters. Dividing that distance by a propagation speed of 2 x 10^8 meters per second gives a propagation delay of about 0.028 seconds, or 28 milliseconds, for the signal to travel one way. Doubling that for a round trip gives roughly 56 milliseconds contributed by propagation delay alone, before adding any transmission, queuing, or processing delay at either end. This lines up well with real-world transatlantic ping times, which commonly land somewhere in the 70 to 90 millisecond range once those other delay components are added on top of the propagation delay itself.

It is worth being precise about how propagation delay differs from transmission delay, since the two are easy to confuse but describe different things entirely. Transmission delay is how long it takes to push all the bits of a packet onto the link in the first place, calculated as the packet's size divided by the link's bandwidth, so a larger packet or a slower link both increase transmission delay. Propagation delay, by contrast, has nothing to do with packet size or bandwidth at all. It depends only on distance and the medium's propagation speed, which is why upgrading a link to a higher bandwidth reduces transmission delay but does absolutely nothing to reduce propagation delay.

This is the reason distance has a hard, physical floor on how fast any connection can ever feel, no matter how much money or bandwidth is thrown at it. A server in Sydney simply cannot respond to a request from London faster than the propagation delay across roughly 17,000 kilometers of cable allows, since that portion of the delay is set by geography and the speed of light, not by engineering choices, which is exactly why services aiming for low latency place their infrastructure physically close to their users rather than trying to engineer around distance itself.
